Sample text:
---
There is a drawer in most homes that is not for anything. Cables, mostly. A charger with a barrel plug and a lump of ferrite near the end, like a snake that ate something. Mini-USB, which was going to be the standard forever. A SCART lead, thick as a garden hose, its connector shaped like a small ironing board. An adapter that converts something to something, both ends now unidentified. Three cables identical to one another, none of which, you are certain, is the one you need.

Ask why it's kept and you'll get: *you never know.* This is a lie, but a load-bearing one. The economics don't work. The rent on two cubic inches of drawer is trivial, sure, but so is replacement — four dollars, ten minutes, delivered tomorrow. The probability that you will urgently need a SCART lead in 2031 and be unable to obtain one is smaller than the probability you'll urgently need a working fax. This is not insurance. Insurance is what you buy after doing the math. This is something else, wearing insurance's coat.

First guess: the drawer is addressed to a future version of you. That person is more capable. They have a workshop, or at least a shelf, and the kind of weekend that contains a project. They fix things. They own a soldering iron and know which end of it to hold. You are furnishing their life in advance, the way a parent buys a coat one size up.

The trouble is that you're also awful to this same person. You send them your unpaid bills, the letter you should have written in March, the dentist appointment, the body you didn't stretch. Future-you is simultaneously an heir you're endowing and a bin you're filling. That inconsistency should make us suspicious of the theory. We aren't modelling a person. We're using a placeholder to hold whatever we can't hold ourselves.

And the contents give it away. Those cables don't point forward. Each one points at a specific object that is no longer in your house. The camcorder. The phone that took a SIM the size of a postage stamp. The external drive with the wedding photos on it — and the other external drive, with nothing on it, which you also kept. These are not supplies. They're the surviving halves of pairs.

The older form of this is the button jar. Buttons cut off coats before the coats went into the rag bag. Buttons from trousers worn through at the knee in 1974. A button outlives its garment by forty years and has no possible use for its original purpose ever again, and still it goes in the jar, because a button implies mending, and mending implies that the world is the sort of place that continues — that there will be a shirt, and a hole, and an afternoon in which to close it. The jar is optimism in a form so small that nobody can argue with it.

Here is the diagnostic. Someone else clears the drawer. A partner, a kid helping you move, someone tidying with the brutal efficiency of love. It takes them ninety seconds. Everything goes into a bin bag, including the thing with the yellow tip, and you experience a rage wildly out of proportion to four dollars of obsolete copper. The disproportion is the tell. Nobody has ever been that angry about a genuinely replaceable object.

What's stored in there isn't possibility. It's refusal — a small, deniable refusal to concede that a period is finished. Throwing out the camcorder cable means signing something. Not mourning the camcorder, which is already gone, sold at a car boot sale or dead in a box in the loft; you made peace with that years ago. It's mourning the person who used to film things. Who thought the school play was worth recording in full, all forty minutes, including the eleven before it started. That person had a specific relationship to time: they believed the present was worth capturing because it would later be scarce. You don't do that anymore. Not because you've become wise. Because you got tired, or the kids stopped being cute in that particular way, or the filming became a thing you did instead of a thing you watched.

The cable is the last physical evidence that this person existed. And it's evidence of a kind nobody can accuse you of sentimentality over. That's the genius of the arrangement. Grief in installments of two cubic inches. You can't be caught mourning a Nokia. No one brings a casserole. There is no card for *the version of you who used to record everything has died,* and so the feeling goes into the drawer with the ferrite lump and the SCART lead, where it can be visited without comment, disguised as thrift.

Now, a correction, because it would be easy to make everything mean something, and that's a vice. Most of the drawer is just friction. Those three identical USB-C cables aren't a memorial to anything; they're the residue of a Tuesday when the bin was downstairs and you were not. Sorting requires decisions, decisions cost glucose, and the drawer is where you put things to avoid paying. Laziness is the majority shareholder here. Sentiment owns a minority stake and takes all the credit.

But you can separate them. Pick up a cable and try to name its device. If you can't — if it's just a black thing with a lump — that's friction, and it can go. If the name arrives instantly, whole, with the room it lived in and the sound of its fan, that's not a cable. That's a headstone you've been dusting.

I don't think knowing this empties the drawer. Understanding a mechanism has never once dissolved it; you can see exactly what you're doing and keep doing it, which is more or less the human condition and the reason therapy takes years rather than an afternoon. You can hold the thing with the yellow tip, know precisely which year it belongs to and who you were in it, understand that the four dollars is not the point and never was — and put it back.

Though maybe further toward the front. Somewhere you'll see it.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective essay turns an ordinary drawer of obsolete cables into an account of grief, memory, and the self we leave behind.

## Grounded reading
The voice is witty and conversational, but its humor keeps giving way to tenderness: obsolete plugs become “surviving halves of pairs,” and the drawer becomes a discreet place to grieve for former versions of oneself. The piece is careful not to sentimentalize everything; its admission that most clutter is simply friction makes the more charged objects feel earned. It invites the reader to inspect an everyday habit without shame, and to notice what a seemingly useless object might be preserving.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds obsolete technology, household clutter, and the quiet persistence of memory. Its central moral claim is that keeping things can be a small refusal to accept that a period of life is over, though the essay also insists that laziness accounts for most of the drawer. The mood moves from dry comedy toward elegy, then ends with a modest, unresolved act of keeping the cable.

## Evidence line
> The jar is optimism in a form so small that nobody can argue with it.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The essay is coherent and distinctive, repeatedly turning ordinary objects into emotionally precise metaphors while tempering that impulse with humor and practical skepticism.
